title: Chapter 118 — The Quadrant
paragraphs: The season for the Line, the equator, finally came close. Every day, whenever Ahab came up from his cabin and looked aloft, the watchful helmsman would make a show of handling his spokes, and the eager sailors would hurry to the braces and stand there with all their eyes converging on the nailed doubloon, impatient for the order to point the ship's prow toward the equator. In due time the order came. It was nearly high noon, and Ahab, seated in the bow of his boat, which was hoisted high, was about to take his usual daily sighting of the sun to find his latitude.

Now, in that Japanese sea, the days in summer are floods of brilliance. That unblinkingly vivid Japanese sun seems the blazing focus of the glassy ocean's immeasurable burning-glass. The sky looks lacquered; there are no clouds; the horizon floats; and this nakedness of unrelieved radiance is like the unbearable splendors of God's throne. It was well that Ahab's quadrant, the instrument for measuring the sun's height, was fitted with colored glasses through which to sight that solar fire. So, swinging his seated body to the roll of the ship, and with his astrological-looking instrument to his eye, he held that posture for some moments to catch the exact instant when the sun should reach its precise meridian. Meanwhile, as his whole attention was absorbed, the Parsee was kneeling beneath him on the ship's deck, and with his face thrown up like Ahab's, was eyeing the same sun with him; only his eyelids half hooded his eyes, and his wild face was subdued to an earthly passionlessness. At length the desired observation was taken; and with his pencil on his ivory leg, Ahab soon calculated what his latitude must be at that precise instant. Then, falling into a moment's reverie, he looked up again toward the sun and murmured to himself: "You sea-mark! You high and mighty Pilot! You tell me truly where I am now — but can you cast the least hint of where I shall be? Or can you tell where some other thing besides me is living this moment? Where is Moby Dick? This instant you must be eyeing him. These eyes of mine look into the very eye that is even now beholding him; aye, and into the eye that is even now equally beholding the objects on the unknown, far side of you, you sun!"

Then, gazing at his quadrant and handling one after another its many cabalistic contrivances, he pondered again, and muttered: "Foolish toy! Babies' plaything of haughty Admirals, and Commodores, and Captains; the world brags of you, of your cunning and might; but what, after all, can you do, except tell the poor, pitiful point where you yourself happen to be on this wide planet, and the hand that holds you — no! not one jot more! You cannot tell where one drop of water or one grain of sand will be tomorrow noon; and yet with your impotence you insult the sun! Science! Curse you, you vain toy; and cursed be all the things that cast man's eyes aloft to that heaven whose live vividness only scorches him, as these old eyes are even now scorched with your light, O sun! By nature, the glances of man's eyes are level with this earth's horizon; not shot from the crown of his head, as if God had meant him to gaze on his firmament. Curse you, you quadrant!" dashing it to the deck. "No longer will I guide my earthly way by you; the level ship's compass, and the level dead-reckoning, by log and by line — it is these that shall guide me, and show me my place on the sea. Aye," stepping down from the boat to the deck, "thus I trample on you, you paltry thing that feebly points on high; thus I split and destroy you!"

As the frantic old man thus spoke and thus trampled with his live and dead feet, a sneering triumph that seemed meant for Ahab, and a fatalistic despair that seemed meant for himself — these passed over the mute, motionless Parsee's face. Unobserved he rose and glided away; while, awestruck by the aspect of their commander, the sailors clustered together on the forecastle, until Ahab, pacing the deck in agitation, shouted out: "To the braces! Up helm! — square in!"

In an instant the yards swung around, and as the ship half-spun on her heel, her three graceful masts, firmly seated and standing upright on her long ribbed hull, looked like the three Horatii pirouetting on a single horse strong enough to carry them all.
Standing between the knightheads (the timbers on either side of the bowsprit), Starbuck watched the Pequod's tumultuous way, and Ahab's also, as he went lurching along the deck.

"I have sat by a thick coal fire and watched it glowing, full of its tormented, flaming life, and I have seen it fade at last, down, down, to the dumbest dust. Old man of the oceans! Of all this fiery life of yours, what will finally be left but one little heap of ashes!"

"Aye," cried Stubb, "but sea-coal ashes — mind you that, Mr. Starbuck — sea-coal, not your common charcoal. Well, well; I heard Ahab mutter, 'Here someone thrusts these cards into these old hands of mine; swears that I must play them, and no others.' And damn me, Ahab, but you act right; live in the game, and die in it!"
